name: Year 11 Mechanics – Key Terms and Definitions

cards.definition: A quantity that has magnitude (size) only, with no direction.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
The size or amount of a physical quantity.
The way in which a vector quantity acts or moves.
The single vector that represents the combined effect of two or more vectors.
The total length of the path travelled by an object.
The straight-line change in position from the starting point to the finishing point, including direction.
The distance travelled per unit of time.
The rate of change of displacement; speed in a particular direction.
The rate at which velocity changes over time.
A push or pull that can change an object's motion.
The force that attracts objects towards one another. Near Earth, it causes objects to accelerate downwards.
The duration over which an event or motion occurs.
The amount of matter in an object.
A graph showing an object's position or displacement over time. Its gradient represents velocity.
A graph showing how an object's velocity changes over time. Its gradient represents acceleration.
The steepness of a graph, calculated as the change in the vertical value divided by the change in the horizontal value.
The area between a graph and the horizontal axis. On a velocity-time graph, it represents displacement.
The velocity an object has at the beginning of a period of motion.
The velocity an object has at the end of a period of motion.
Motion where gravity is the only force considered to be acting on an object.
The energy an object has because it is moving.
Stored energy an object has because of its position or height.
The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed.
Energy transferred when a force causes an object to move through a displacement.
The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
The use of relationships between angles and sides of triangles to calculate unknown values.
A trigonometric ratio calculated using opposite ÷ hypotenuse.
A trigonometric ratio calculated using adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.
A trigonometric ratio calculated using opposite ÷ adjacent.
Speed
Acceleration
Final velocity
Displacement
Final velocity without needing time
Kinetic energy
Gravitational potential energy
Work
Power
Resultant vector magnitude
Electrostatic attraction between positively charged metal particles and delocalised electrons in a metallic lattice.
Electrons that are not attached to one particular atom and can move throughout a structure.
Bonding where attraction acts in all directions, allowing particles to shift while maintaining attraction.
Strong electrostatic attraction between positively charged cations and negatively charged anions.
A strong attraction formed when atoms share a pair of electrons.
A large continuous structure of atoms connected by strong covalent bonds.
A repeating three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.
A repeating structure of positive metal particles surrounded by delocalised electrons.
Attractive forces acting between separate molecules.
Attractive forces or bonds acting between atoms within the same particle or molecule.
The ability of a solid to be hammered, bent or moulded into a different shape without breaking.
The ability of a material to be drawn into a wire without breaking.
The tendency of a material to break or shatter when sufficient force is applied.
The ability of a substance to allow charged particles to move through it and carry electrical current.
The ability of a solute to dissolve in a solvent to form a solution.
Energy associated with the attractive forces holding oppositely charged ions together within an ionic lattice.
A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge, producing regions of partial positive and negative charge.
A separation of electrical charge that creates a partially positive region and a partially negative region.
Electrons in the outer shell of an atom that are involved in chemical bonding.
A pair of valence electrons located on an atom that is not involved in a covalent bond.
A region of electron density associated with a bond between atoms.
A region around an atom where negatively charged electrons are located.
The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms around a central atom in a molecule.
A molecular arrangement involving four bonding regions around a central atom, arranged for maximum separation.
A molecular shape involving three bonding regions and one lone pair around the central atom.
An organic compound made entirely from carbon and hydrogen atoms.
A hydrocarbon in which the carbon atoms have the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms attached.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon-carbon double or triple bond and therefore not having the maximum possible hydrogen atoms.
A saturated hydrocarbon containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon triple bond.
A separation technique that separates components of a mixture according to differences in boiling point or volatility.
A measure of how readily a substance vaporises; more volatile substances enter the gas phase more easily.
A reaction where atoms are added across a multiple bond, producing a more saturated molecule.
A rule used to predict the major product when an unsymmetrical molecule is added across an unsymmetrical alkene.
The product formed in the greatest amount when a reaction can produce multiple structural products.
A possible product formed in a smaller amount than the major product.
A chemical reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen and releases energy.
Combustion occurring with sufficient oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water from the fuels considered in the exam.
Combustion occurring with limited oxygen, allowing products such as carbon monoxide and carbon to form.
A chemical reaction that releases energy to the surroundings.
The energy change associated with a chemical reaction; the exam uses a negative ΔH to indicate energy release.
The principle that matter is not created or destroyed during a chemical reaction.
A system in which matter cannot escape, allowing the total mass before and after a reaction to be compared.
A reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form one product.
A reaction in which one reactant breaks down to form two or more products.
A reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water.
A reaction involving soluble ionic substances that produces an insoluble solid.
An insoluble solid formed from substances reacting in solution.
A substance capable of donating hydrogen ions, H⁺, and producing a conjugate base.
An acid that fully dissociates into ions in solution.
An acid that only partially dissociates, establishing an equilibrium between ionised and unionised forms.
The process in which a substance separates into ions when in solution.
The species remaining after an acid has donated a hydrogen ion.
A condition in which forward and reverse processes occur, represented in the exam using a reversible arrow.
An acid capable of donating two hydrogen ions.
The lowering of ocean pH associated in the exam with CO₂ reacting with seawater and increasing acidity.
A measure related in the exam to the number of successful particle collisions occurring each second.
The amount of time required for a reaction to reach completion.
The idea that reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy and an appropriate orientation for a successful reaction.
A collision between reactant particles that has sufficient energy and suitable orientation to produce a reaction.
The minimum energy requirement that must be overcome for a chemical reaction to occur.
A substance that increases reaction rate by providing a pathway with a lower activation energy.
The amount of a substance present within a particular volume of solution.
The amount of a solid reactant exposed and available for collisions with other reactant particles.
A different structural form of the same chemical element in the same physical state.
A carbon allotrope consisting of covalently bonded layers with delocalised electrons and weaker attractions between layers.
A carbon allotrope consisting of a three-dimensional network of carbon atoms connected by strong covalent bonds.
A large molecule made from many smaller repeating units linked together in long chains.
A smaller molecule capable of joining with other monomers to form a polymer.
A chemical reaction in which monomers join together to form a polymer.
The structural section of a polymer that repeats throughout the polymer chain.
A manufactured polymer, such as polyethylene, Kevlar or nylon in the exam classification.
A naturally occurring polymer, such as DNA, silk or collagen in the exam classification.
The basic building block of all living things.
A small structure inside a cell that has a specific job.
The part of the cell that contains DNA and controls cell activities.
A thin layer that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
A strong outer layer that supports and protects plant cells.
The jelly-like substance where many cell activities take place.
A storage space in a plant cell that holds water and other substances.
An organelle where photosynthesis takes place.
The green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
Organelles where cellular respiration releases usable energy.
A strong carbohydrate that makes up much of the plant cell wall.
The genetic information that provides instructions for cells.
A group of similar cells working together to perform a function.
A structure made of different tissues working together.
A cell adapted to perform a particular job.
The plant organ that absorbs water and minerals and helps anchor the plant.
Supports the plant and transports water, minerals and sugars.
The main organ where photosynthesis takes place.
A structure that develops from a flower and helps protect and disperse seeds.
A structure containing a young plant that can grow into a new plant.
Vascular tissue that transports water and minerals from the roots upwards.
Vascular tissue that transports sugars around the plant.
Plant tissue responsible for transporting substances through the plant.
The inner leaf tissue where most photosynthesis occurs.
Tightly packed leaf cells containing many chloroplasts.
Loosely packed leaf cells with air spaces that help gas exchange.
The outer protective layer of a leaf.
A thin, waxy layer that reduces water loss from the leaf.
Cells that support the function of phloem tissue.
Perforated structures between phloem cells that allow sugars to move through.
A layer of tissue between xylem and phloem in dicot plants.
The central part of a root or stem containing vascular tissues.
A tiny opening, usually on the underside of a leaf, that allows gas exchange.
The plural of stoma; the openings in leaves.
Specialised cells that control the opening and closing of stomata.
The movement of gases into and out of a plant.
The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through its leaves.
The pulling force created when water evaporates from leaves, drawing more water upwards.
The process where liquid water changes into water vapour.
The movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
The attraction between water molecules that makes them stick together.
The attraction between water molecules and other surfaces, such as xylem walls.
The pressure of water inside a plant cell pushing against its cell wall.
When a plant cell has lost water and become less firm.
When a plant becomes droopy due to a loss of water and reduced cell pressure.
The movement of substances from one part of a plant to another.
Movement of substances without the use of cellular energy.
Movement of substances that requires energy from the cell.
The movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution towards a more concentrated solution.
A barrier that allows some substances through but blocks others.
The amount of a substance in a particular volume or space.
A difference in concentration between two areas.
A substance that is dissolved in a liquid.
The liquid that dissolves another substance.
A solution containing a relatively small amount of dissolved substance.
A solution containing a relatively large amount of dissolved substance.
The part of a plant where sugars are produced or released into the phloem.
The part of a plant where sugars are used or stored.
The movement of sugars through phloem due to differences in pressure.
The process where plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
The process where cells break down glucose to release usable energy.
A simple sugar produced during photosynthesis and used in respiration.
A gas released during photosynthesis and used during aerobic respiration.
A gas absorbed by plants and used during photosynthesis.
An organism that makes its own food.
An organism that produces its own food and provides energy for other organisms.
A molecule that provides usable energy for cell activities.
Energy stored in chemical substances, such as glucose.
The substances needed for a process to take place.
The substances made by a chemical process.
The organelle where photosynthesis occurs.
An organelle where cellular respiration takes place.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
The two new cells produced through cell division.
Plant tissue where cells actively divide and produce new growth.
The growing end of a root where many cells divide.
An increase in the size of an organism through cell division and cell enlargement.
The replacement of damaged cells and tissues.
The process where a seed begins to grow into a new plant.
The stages an organism goes through from the beginning of its life until it reproduces.
A flowering plant whose seed produces one first leaf during germination.
A flowering plant whose seed produces two first leaves during germination.
The movement of seeds away from the parent plant.
A substance needed by a plant for healthy growth.
A substance added to soil to provide nutrients for plants.
A naturally occurring substance that plants absorb from the soil.
A feature that helps an organism survive in its environment.
A plant's growth response towards or away from a stimulus.
A plant's growth response to light.
A plant's growth response to gravity.
The amount of water accessible to a plant.
The amount of carbon dioxide available for photosynthesis.
A factor that restricts the rate of a process, such as photosynthesis or growth.
